title: Where We Monitor Matters: Monitoring-Network Composition and Bayesian River-Network Inference for Phosphorus Exceedance in English Rivers
content: Routine water-quality monitoring sites are selected purposively, whereas probability-based surveillance networks sample river reaches by design. We compared England's probability-based River Surveillance Network (RSN; 679 sites) with routine statutory monitoring (1,153 sites) for reactive phosphorus in 2023–2024. A Bayesian measurement-level model accounted for observation-specific reporting limits, defined exceedance using the latent calendar-year arithmetic mean, and represented geographical structure through management units, a smooth spatial field and a tail-up river-network covariance. Routine site-years exceeded 0.05, 0.10 and 0.20 mg P L\( ^{-1} \) 16–22 percentage points more often than RSN site-years. After standardisation to a common set of 2,256 site-years, the differences narrowed to 2–3 percentage points (0.025, 95% CrI 0.004–0.050, at 0.10 mg P L\( ^{-1} \)), corresponding to a routine-site offset of approximately 8% in concentration. Accounting for river-network dependence halved the contrast remaining after hierarchical and spatial adjustment, because routine sites concentrate on a few phosphorus-enriched river systems. The residual contrast would disappear if unmonitored reaches were approximately 10% more enriched than the RSN sites representing them. In held-out comparisons that did not satisfy all pre-specified validation criteria, the river-network term provided no material predictive advantage in unmonitored catchments, while an apparent improvement on monitored rivers remained unconfirmed. Across 68,822 km of mapped rivers, the model-based probability that the reference-level annual mean exceeded 0.10 mg P L\( ^{-1} \) was 0.35 (95% CrI 0.33–0.37), compared with 0.46 across monitored site-years; plausible residual selection shifted this estimate by approximately \( \pm \)0.06. Network disagreement mainly reflects where networks sample, so assessments should define their target population.
